notes.b: Chemists first described oxidation and reduction in terms of oxygen and hydrogen. These definitions are easy to picture, but they turned out to be too narrow.
points: Oxidation (early definition) is the addition of oxygen to a substance, for example C + O₂ → CO₂ and 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.
Reduction (early definition) is the removal of oxygen from a substance, or the addition of hydrogen, for example CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O.
In that example, black copper(II) oxide turns to pink-brown copper when hydrogen is passed over it while heated, so you can see the reduction happen.
The name “reduction” comes from extracting metals from their ores (the rocks the metal is mined in): the ore is reduced to a smaller mass of metal as the oxygen is removed.

The oxygen definitions cover only some reactions. Many redox reactions (reactions with both oxidation and reduction) involve no oxygen or hydrogen at all, for example sodium and chlorine, so a broader definition is needed.
notes.tip: Use the extraction of metals from ores only to explain where the word “reduction” comes from; metal extraction itself is not on the specification.

notes.h: Oxidation and reduction as electron transfer
notes.b: The broader definition follows electrons (the tiny negative particles in atoms), which works for every redox reaction, with or without oxygen. Whatever one substance loses, another must gain.
points: Oxidation is the loss of electrons; reduction is the gain of electrons. Memory aid: OIL RIG (Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain).
Example: 2Na(s) + Cl₂(g) → 2NaCl(s). Each sodium atom loses one electron, Na → Na⁺ + e⁻, which is oxidation.
In the same reaction each chlorine atom gains one electron, Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻, which is reduction. Group 1 metals react with chlorine to form white ionic chlorides.
A half-equation shows one process with its electrons, for example Zn(s) → Zn²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ (oxidation) and Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ → Cu(s) (reduction).
Electrons appear on the right in an oxidation and on the left in a reduction, which lets you classify any half-equation at a glance.
notes.tip: To classify a half-equation, look at which side the electrons are on: right means oxidation, left means reduction. If asked to define oxidation and reduction, answer in terms of electron transfer.

notes.h: Redox reactions: oxidation and reduction together
notes.b: Oxidation never happens alone. A redox reaction (the name joins reduction and oxidation) is one in which both take place at the same time.
points: A redox reaction is one in which oxidation and reduction take place together.
They must happen together because electrons lost by one substance can't disappear, so another substance must gain them; the number lost equals the number gained.
Example: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s), from zinc in copper(II) sulfate solution. Each zinc atom transfers two electrons to a copper(II) ion.
You can see this reaction: the zinc becomes coated with brown copper and the blue colour of the solution fades as Cu²⁺ ions are used up.
notes.tip: Exams ask how many electrons are transferred. In Zn + Cu²⁺ it is two per zinc atom, and the number lost always equals the number gained.

notes.b: Each substance in a redox reaction has a second name that describes what it does to its partner. The agent is the one that causes the change in the other substance, and it undergoes the opposite change itself.
points: An oxidising agent brings about oxidation in another substance by accepting its electrons; the oxidising agent is itself reduced.
A reducing agent brings about reduction in another substance by giving it electrons; the reducing agent is itself oxidised.
To identify them, find the species (the atom, ion or molecule) that loses electrons: it is oxidised and is the reducing agent. The species that gains electrons is reduced and is the oxidising agent.
In Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu, zinc is the reducing agent (oxidised, Zn → Zn²⁺) and the copper(II) ion, from copper(II) sulfate, is the oxidising agent (reduced, Cu²⁺ → Cu).
Name the species, not the element: the oxidising agent is Cu²⁺ (or copper(II) sulfate), not “copper”.
The sulfate ion takes no part in that reaction; it is a spectator ion (an ion that is present but is not changed).
notes.tip: The oxidising agent is reduced and the reducing agent is oxidised; students often swap them. Name the species (Cu²⁺ or copper(II) sulfate), not just the element in words.

notes.b: Apply the same test each time: who loses electrons, and who gains them? These examples show it with a metal and a non-metal, and then with a reaction in solution where you can see a colour change.
points: In 2K + Cl₂ → 2KCl, potassium is oxidised (it is the reducing agent) and chlorine is reduced (it is the oxidising agent).
Bromine water oxidises sulfite ions to sulfate ions, and the orange-yellow colour of the bromine disappears: SO₃²⁻(aq) + Br₂(aq) + H₂O(l) → SO₄²⁻(aq) + 2Br⁻(aq) + 2H⁺(aq).
In the bromine reaction, bromine is the oxidising agent and sulfite is the reducing agent. The colour fades because the bromine is used up as colourless bromide ions, Br⁻.
Halogen displacement reactions (a more reactive halogen taking the place of a less reactive one in a compound) are another example. There is more on this in Families and trends in the periodic table.
notes.tip: Exams give equations such as Na + Cl₂, Zn + Cu²⁺ and K + Cl₂ and ask you to name the species oxidised and reduced and the two agents.

notes.b: Redox chemistry is used in the home, in medicine and in food. Oxidising agents are used to bleach and to kill germs, while reducing agents are used to stop other things being oxidised.
points: Many bleaches and disinfectants are oxidising agents: they oxidise coloured substances to colourless ones, or kill microorganisms (tiny living things such as bacteria) by oxidising them.
Hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) is an oxidising agent used to bleach hair.
Sodium hypochlorite (NaOCl, containing the hypochlorite ion ClO⁻) is household bleach.
Chlorine (Cl₂) disinfects drinking water. There is more on this in Treating drinking water.
Iodine solution (tincture of iodine) is an antiseptic (a germ-killer) for cuts.
Sulfur dioxide (SO₂, food additive E220) is a reducing agent used as a preservative, for example in wine and dried fruit, because it prevents oxidation of the food.
Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) is an antioxidant, which means it acts as a reducing agent: it is oxidised in place of other substances.

notes.b: Metals tend to react with their surroundings and turn back into compounds. This is oxidation of the metal, and for iron and steel it has a familiar name, rusting.
points: Corrosion is the unwanted conversion of a metal to one of its compounds by reaction with its environment, for example oxygen and water; the metal is oxidised.
Rusting is the corrosion of iron and steel. It needs both oxygen and water: iron is oxidised, Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ and then to iron(III), while oxygen is reduced.
Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide (iron(III) oxide with water bound in), Fe₂O₃·xH₂O, a brown flaky solid.
Salt, for example from sea spray or road salt, speeds up rusting.
Copper corrodes slowly in air to form a green layer of copper compounds (verdigris, or a patina), as on copper roofs and the copper skin of the Statue of Liberty.
Aluminium is a reactive metal but resists corrosion because a thin layer of aluminium oxide, Al₂O₃, forms on its surface and sticks firmly, stopping air and water reaching the metal underneath.
notes.tip: If asked what corrosion is, say it is the unwanted conversion of a metal to one of its compounds, and that the metal is oxidised.

notes.b: Rusting needs oxygen and water, so the simplest protection is to keep both away from the iron. Barrier methods do this with a coating.
points: Barrier methods keep out oxygen and water: painting, coating with plastic, oil or grease (for moving parts), and plating with a less reactive metal.
Examples of plating are tin on steel food cans and chromium on taps.
Once the barrier is scratched, the iron underneath rusts.
With tin plating, the exposed iron rusts even faster than bare iron, because iron is more reactive than tin.
notes.tip: Exams ask how painting and coating with another metal protect iron: they act as a barrier that keeps out oxygen and water.

notes.h: Preventing corrosion: galvanising and sacrificial protection
notes.b: A second approach uses a more reactive metal, which is oxidised in place of the iron. Even if the coating is damaged, the iron stays protected.
points: Galvanising is coating iron or steel with zinc, for example buckets, wheelbarrows and fencing.

Zinc is more easily oxidised than iron (higher in the electrochemical series, the list of metals ranked by reactivity), so even if the coating is scratched the zinc is oxidised instead of the iron. There is more on this in The electrochemical series and displacement.
Sacrificial protection: a block of a more reactive metal, zinc or magnesium, is attached to steel ship hulls or underground pipes.
The sacrificial block is oxidised (corrodes) instead of the steel and is replaced from time to time.
notes.tip: For galvanising, say that zinc is more easily oxidised than iron, so the zinc is oxidised instead, even when scratched. This is the opposite of tin plating.

notes.b: Burning fuels and releasing energy from food in your cells are both oxidations. In each, oxygen is the oxidising agent.
points: Combustion (burning) of fuels is oxidation: the fuel is oxidised and oxygen is the oxidising agent (it is reduced), for example CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l). There is more on the energy released in Combustion and heats of combustion.
Respiration is the oxidation of glucose in cells to release energy: C₆H₁₂O₆(aq) + 6O₂(g) → 6CO₂(g) + 6H₂O(l).
In respiration glucose is oxidised and oxygen is reduced.
Photosynthesis (the process in plants that makes glucose) is the reverse, in which carbon dioxide is reduced to glucose.

notes.b: Iron is a nutrient, and the form of iron in a tablet matters. Redox chemistry explains which form is used and why vitamin C helps.
points: Iron is needed to make haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in the blood; a lack of iron causes iron-deficiency anaemia (too few healthy red blood cells), treated with iron tablets.
Iron tablets contain iron as iron(II), Fe²⁺ (for example iron(II) sulfate), because iron(II) is the form the body absorbs best.
Fe²⁺ is easily oxidised to Fe³⁺ by oxygen in the air: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻. This is a problem, because Fe³⁺ is not absorbed as well.
Vitamin C (ascorbic acid), a reducing agent, helps the body absorb iron: it reduces Fe³⁺ to Fe²⁺ (Fe³⁺ + e⁻ → Fe²⁺), so iron tablets are often taken with vitamin C or orange juice.

The iron(II) in a tablet can be measured by titration (adding one solution from a burette to another until the reaction is just complete) with potassium manganate(VII), which oxidises Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺. There is more on this in Redox titrations and iron tablets.

notes.h: Oxidation numbers: meaning and use (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Electron transfer is easy to see in ionic reactions but harder in covalent ones, where electrons are shared. Oxidation numbers give a way to track electrons in every case.
points: The oxidation number (oxidation state) of an atom is the charge it has, or appears to have, when the electrons in its bonds are assigned according to a set of rules.
In a covalent bond the shared electrons are given to the more electronegative atom (the one that attracts the bonding electrons more strongly).
Oxidation numbers are not real charges in covalent substances; they are a bookkeeping tool for tracking electron transfer.
Oxidation numbers are written with the sign first (+2, −1), unlike ionic charges (2+, 1−).
Oxidation is an increase in oxidation number; reduction is a decrease in oxidation number. The size of the change is the number of electrons lost or gained per atom.
Oxidation numbers are assigned only for compounds of the first 36 elements (hydrogen to krypton).
Oxidation numbers can also be used to balance redox equations. There is more on this in Balancing redox equations.
notes.tip: Write oxidation numbers sign first (+2) and ionic charges number first (2+). Be ready to define oxidation and reduction in terms of oxidation number as well as electrons.

notes.h: Oxidation numbers in reactions: worked examples (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Once you know how oxidation numbers change, you can pick out what is oxidised and reduced and name the agents, even when no ions are involved.
points: Example: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Hydrogen goes from 0 to +1 (oxidised; H₂ is the reducing agent); oxygen goes from 0 to −2 (reduced; O₂ is the oxidising agent).
Example: Cu + 2H₂SO₄ (concentrated) → CuSO₄ + SO₂ + 2H₂O. Copper goes from 0 to +2 (oxidised; copper is the reducing agent).
In the same reaction sulfur goes from +6 in H₂SO₄ to +4 in SO₂ (reduced; sulfuric acid is the oxidising agent).
The sulfur that ends up in CuSO₄ stays at +6, so only one of the two sulfur atoms in 2H₂SO₄ is reduced.

notes.h: Rules for assigning oxidation numbers: the basic rules (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Oxidation numbers are assigned by following rules in order. The first four deal with elements, ions and the totals that must be reached.
points: Rule 1: an uncombined element has oxidation number 0, for example Zn, Fe, Na, O₂, Cl₂, P₄.
Rule 2: a simple (monatomic, single-atom) ion has an oxidation number equal to its charge, for example Na⁺ +1, Mg²⁺ +2, Fe²⁺ +2, Fe³⁺ +3, Cl⁻ −1, Br⁻ −1, O²⁻ −2.
Rule 3: the oxidation numbers in a neutral compound add up to 0, for example NaCl: (+1) + (−1) = 0; H₂O: 2(+1) + (−2) = 0.
Rule 4: the oxidation numbers in a polyatomic ion (an ion made of several atoms) add up to the charge on the ion, for example NO₃⁻: N + 3(−2) = −1, so N = +5.
Group 1 metals are always +1 and group 2 metals +2 in their compounds, which gives you known values to solve from.

notes.h: Rules for assigning oxidation numbers: oxygen, hydrogen, halogens and non-metals (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Oxygen, hydrogen and the halogens usually have a fixed value, but each has exceptions. The exceptions all follow from which atom is more electronegative.
points: Rule 5: oxygen is −2 in its compounds, except in peroxides (H₂O₂, Na₂O₂), where it is −1 (2(+1) + 2(O) = 0, so O = −1), and in OF₂, where it is +2.
In OF₂ fluorine is more electronegative than oxygen, so fluorine takes the electrons and is −1.
Rule 6: hydrogen is +1 in its compounds, except in metal hydrides (for example NaH, CaH₂), where it is −1.
In a metal hydride hydrogen is more electronegative than the metal, so the bonding electrons are assigned to hydrogen; NaH contains the H⁻ ion.
Rule 7: fluorine is always −1 in its compounds; the other halogens are −1 except when bonded to a more electronegative element (oxygen or fluorine).
For example Cl is +1 in NaClO and Cl₂O, +5 in ClO₃⁻, and +7 in Cl₂O₇ and ClO₄⁻.
Rule 8: in a compound of two non-metals not covered above, the more electronegative element takes its usual negative value and the other is calculated, for example CS₂: S = −2, so C = +4.
Pauling electronegativities (a scale of how strongly an atom attracts bonding electrons; see “Electronegativity and bond type”): H 2.20, Na 0.93, Ca 1.00, S 2.58, C 2.55, F 3.98, O 3.44.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to explain why hydrogen is −1 in metal hydrides and oxygen is +2 in OF₂, and these exceptions are asked often. In both cases, say which element is more electronegative and so takes the electrons. Peroxides give oxygen −1.

notes.h: Assigning oxidation numbers: method and worked examples (Higher Level only)
notes.b: With the rules, you can find any unknown oxidation number by simple algebra. The total must come to 0 for a compound, or to the charge for an ion.
points: Method: write the known values from the rules, then solve for the unknown so that the total equals 0 for a compound, or the charge of the ion.
Example: in KMnO₄, (+1) + Mn + 4(−2) = 0, so Mn = +7.
K₂Cr₂O₇: 2(+1) + 2Cr + 7(−2) = 0, so 2Cr = +12 and Cr = +6; in Cr³⁺ (for example chromium(III) sulfate) Cr = +3.
CuSO₄: the sulfate ion is SO₄²⁻, so Cu = +2; in SO₄²⁻, S + 4(−2) = −2, so S = +6 and O = −2.
An oxidation number can be a fraction: it is then the average over atoms of the same element, for example in S₄O₆²⁻, 4S + 6(−2) = −2, so S = +2.5.
notes.tip: Exams ask for oxidation numbers such as Cl in NaClO, N in NO₃⁻, Mn in KMnO₄, Cr in a dichromate and P in PO₄³⁻. Write out the sum and solve it.

notes.h: Oxidation numbers of common elements and names (Higher Level only)
notes.b: These values come from the rules above and are worth recognising. The Roman numerals in names also give oxidation numbers directly.
points: Sulfur in other species: H₂S −2; SO₂ +4; SO₃²⁻ +4; H₂SO₄ +6; S₂O₃²⁻ +2.
Nitrogen: NH₃ −3; N₂ 0; NO +2; NO₂ +4; NO₃⁻ and HNO₃ +5.
Carbon: CH₄ −4; CO +2; CO₂ +4; C₂O₄²⁻ +3.
Phosphorus: P₄ 0; PO₄³⁻ +5. Manganese: MnO₂ +4; Mn²⁺ +2.
The Roman numeral in a name gives the oxidation number of the element before it: iron(II) oxide FeO (+2), iron(III) oxide Fe₂O₃ (+3), copper(I) oxide Cu₂O (+1), copper(II) oxide CuO (+2).
Manganese(IV) oxide MnO₂ (+4) is also called manganese dioxide; potassium manganate(VII) KMnO₄ (+7) is also called potassium permanganate; potassium dichromate(VI) K₂Cr₂O₇ (+6).
Iodine is element 53: I₂ is 0 and I⁻ is −1 by rules 1 and 2, but oxidation numbers are not assigned in iodine's compounds, for example iodates, because iodine is beyond the first 36 elements.
notes.tip: Do not assign oxidation numbers in iodine compounds such as iodates; only I₂ (0) and I⁻ (−1) follow from the rules.

keyTerms.definition: The loss of electrons by a substance; in the early definition, the addition of oxygen.
The gain of electrons by a substance; in the early definition, the removal of oxygen or the addition of hydrogen.
A reaction in which oxidation and reduction take place together, so that electrons lost by one substance are gained by another.
A substance that brings about oxidation in another by accepting its electrons, and is itself reduced.
A substance that brings about reduction in another by giving it electrons, and is itself oxidised.
An equation showing one process, oxidation or reduction, with the electrons written in.
An ion that does not change during a reaction and is left out of the ionic equation.
The unwanted conversion of a metal to one of its compounds by reaction with its environment.
Coating iron or steel with zinc so that the zinc protects the iron from corrosion.
Protecting steel by attaching a more reactive metal, which is oxidised instead of the steel.
The charge an atom has, or appears to have, when its bonding electrons are assigned by a set of rules.

questions.prompt: Define oxidation and reduction in terms of electron transfer. In the reaction Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s), identify the oxidising agent and the reducing agent, and state one observation.
questions.model: Oxidation is the loss of electrons and reduction is the gain of electrons. The oxidising agent is the copper(II) ion, Cu²⁺ (from copper(II) sulfate), which accepts electrons and is reduced to copper. The reducing agent is zinc, which gives up two electrons and is oxidised to Zn²⁺. Observation: brown copper forms on the zinc, and the blue colour of the solution fades.

questions.prompt: What is meant by corrosion? Explain how (i) painting and (ii) galvanising protect iron from corrosion, and why galvanised iron is still protected when it is scratched.
questions.model: Corrosion is the unwanted conversion of a metal to one of its compounds by reaction with its environment; the metal is oxidised. Rusting needs both oxygen and water. (i) Paint is a barrier that keeps oxygen and water away from the iron. (ii) Galvanising coats the iron with zinc, which keeps oxygen and water away from the iron in the same way. When the coating is scratched, zinc is more easily oxidised than iron, because zinc is higher in the electrochemical series. The zinc is therefore oxidised instead of the iron, so the iron remains protected.

questions.prompt: Define oxidation number. Assign the oxidation number of (i) chlorine in NaClO, (ii) nitrogen in NO₃⁻, (iii) manganese in KMnO₄. Explain why hydrogen has an oxidation number of −1 in sodium hydride.
questions.model: An oxidation number is the charge an atom has, or appears to have, when the electrons in its bonds are assigned according to a set of rules. (i) Chlorine is +1: (+1) + Cl + (−2) = 0, so Cl = +1. (ii) Nitrogen is +5: N + 3(−2) = −1, so N = +5. (iii) Manganese is +7: (+1) + Mn + 4(−2) = 0, so Mn = +7. Hydrogen is −1 in sodium hydride because hydrogen is more electronegative than sodium, so the bonding electrons are assigned to hydrogen; sodium hydride contains the H⁻ ion.
